title: Ang 957–966: Ramkali ki Var M5
tomorrow: two minstrels sang of one light. so what happened to them?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ang 947: the third Guru's ballad, a war tune carrying a fight inside. Today, the fifth Guru's ballad in the same raga.
screen: `A WAR TUNE, A FIGHT INSIDE.` → `THE FIFTH GURU'S BALLAD.`

segments.voice: At an Anand Karaj, a Sikh wedding, there's a small moment that's easy to miss. Someone in the bride's family places the end of the groom's scarf in her hand: the palla. And right then the musicians sing a line from ang 963 that sounds, at first, like the worst wedding toast ever. I have seen that all relations are false. The bride is holding a scarf, both families are beaming, and the words seem to say the opposite of the whole day. At a wedding? While two families are joining?
screen: `THE END OF THE SCARF.` → `ALL RELATIONS ARE FALSE?` → `AT A WEDDING?`

segments.voice: Here's the whole line, in paraphrase, from Guru Arjan's ballad in Ramkali, Ramkali ki Var, Mahala 5: praise and slander, I have let go of both; I have given up everything else. I have seen all ties as false, so I have caught hold of the hem of your robe. That's the palla: the edge of a garment, the hem. In the old picture, someone holding another's hem has chosen whom to follow and won't let go. So the puzzle solves itself once you ask whose hem it is. Not the groom's. The hem of the One. The line isn't saying family doesn't matter. It's saying no earthly tie can hold a person up forever: people move, change, leave, and die. One hem doesn't slip. So at the palla, two people each take hold of that hem, with a length of cloth between them as the picture of it. The marriage becomes two people holding on to the same Lord, a sturdier knot than holding on only to each other. That's why the line belongs at the wedding, not in spite of it. Even praise and slander are let go: the couple isn't marrying for what people will say. Holding the hem.
screen: `PRAISE AND SLANDER, LET GO.` · `PALLA: THE HEM OF THE ROBE.` · `WHOSE HEM? THE ONE'S.` · `TWO PEOPLE, ONE HEM.` · then, large: `HOLDING THE HEM.`

segments.voice: Take hold of the edge of something: a sleeve, a scarf, the hem of your shirt. Hold it gently for the sit, not gripping, just not letting go, with the hand soft and the breath slow. If you'd like, read the line on ang 963 first.
Ang 957. Where Guru Arjan's ballad in Ramkali begins, the one that holds the palla line on ang 963.
Holding the hem: two people at a wedding, each holding on to the hem of the One. That's it for today.

howItsDone: At the Anand Karaj, a family member places the end of the groom's scarf in the bride's hand while ragis sing Guru Arjan's line 'pallai taindai laagee' from Ramkali ki Var (ang 963); the couple then walk the laavan holding it.
